newsitem.title: UK: Buba rate threat double-edged sword - FX analysts.
newsitem.headline: Buba rate threat double-edged sword - FX analysts.

text.p: The Bundesbank has kept mark bears at bay this week by wielding the threat of the first increase in Germany's key money-market rate in nearly two years.
But analysts said it may have created a rod for its own back.

The central bank has encouraged speculation it could nudge the German securities repurchase rate up from a record low of 3.0 percent if the mark weakens further from the 7-1/2 year lows it set against the dollar on Monday.
Yet, the potency of the threat is already beginning to fade, analysts said.
If a rise in the repo rate was viewed as the beginning of a new interest rate cycle it may trigger concern about German economic recovery and could ultimately encourage sales of marks, they added.

"They have stabilised the mark for a bit but it is a dangerous policy to pursue given the economy cannot sustain higher rates at the moment," said Michael Lewis, senior European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. "They will not want to get into a risky scenario where the market is pushing them into rate rises which are not needed."
He expects the mark to fall below Monday's 1.8490 low in the coming weeks from 1.8305/08 at 1135 GMT.

Concern about a rise in the German repo intensified after the Bundesbank declined to fix the rate for the duration of its four-week summer recess, leaving its options open if mark weakness persisted through August.

The rate rise speculation was fueled further this week by council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick, who said the central bank could tighten money market liquidity in the event of fresh mark losses - possibly by calling a variable rate repo tender.

German exporters have benefited as the mark has tumbled 37 percent from the record highs it scaled against the dollar in March 1995. Much of the rest of the German economy has yet to gather momentum, though, analysts said.

The fiscal belt tightening Germany has undertaken in order to qualify for European economic and monetary union, as well as the current deadlock in passing tax reforms are expected by traders to hamper economic expansion in the months ahead.
This has helped mark bears keep faith.
"There is no real reason to change my mind about the dollar," said Adam Cribben, assistant chief trader at Credit Lyonnais in London.

"The market was worried about the Germans changing their monetary stance, but it is becoming a bit sceptical at this stage given the German economy does not warrant a rate rise and that it does not suit continental Europe as a whole."
Cribben expects the dollar will initially spike down if the Bundesbank does engineer an increase in the repo rate, but he predicted the U.S. currency would not fall below 1.80 marks.
The German central bank is unlikely to want to become embroiled in a tussle with currency traders which economic fundamentals will not allow it to win, analysts said.

"The Germans are quite shrewd and will not get themselves into that situation," said Henry Wilkes, head of trading at Bank Julius Baer. "More likely is that they are using the talk to buy time over August."
The risk, however, is that the dollar bursts through 1.85 marks in the coming weeks, prompting traders to target a move to 1.90 or even 2.0 marks
"We are up here in thin air and a lot of the good news is in the market, but there is no reason to sell it," said Cribben at Credit Lyonnais.
In this case, the German monetary authorities will have to give up their solo efforts to staunch mark weakness and turn to the U.S. for support, analysts said.
"It would carry more credibility, if the U.S. said something, given that so far the U.S. has been more concerned about the dollar/yen," said Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
